what_its_for: Pegfilgrastim-jmdb helps your body make more white blood cells after chemotherapy. Chemotherapy can lower your white blood cell count, which makes it harder for your body to fight infections. This medicine helps reduce your chance of getting a serious infection (called febrile neutropenia) by boosting your immune system.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as a shot (injection) under the skin, usually in the stomach area, upper arm, or thigh. Your doctor or nurse will give you the injection, or they may teach you how to give it to yourself at home. Always use a new needle and syringe for each injection. Do not shake the prefilled syringe. Check the liquid before use — it should be clear and colorless. Do not use it if it looks cloudy, discolored, or has particles in it.
dosing: The usual dose is one injection (6 mg) given once per chemotherapy cycle. It is typically given at least 24 hours after your chemotherapy is finished. Do not give this injection within 14 days before your next chemotherapy treatment. Your doctor will decide the exact timing that is right for you.
missed_dose: If you miss your scheduled injection, call your doctor or nurse right away. Do not try to make up for a missed dose on your own without guidance from your healthcare team. Timing of this medicine is very important, so it is best to keep all your scheduled appointments.
storage: Store this medicine in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Keep it in its original carton to protect it from light. Do not freeze it — if it accidentally freezes, thaw it in the refrigerator and use it right away. You may keep the medicine at room temperature (up to 77°F / 25°C) for no more than 48 hours. Throw away any syringe left at room temperature for more than 48 hours. Keep it out of reach of children. Dispose of used needles and syringes in a puncture-resistant sharps container.
what_to_avoid: Do not receive this injection within 14 days before or 24 hours after chemotherapy. Avoid touching your face or shaking hands with sick people while your white blood cell count is low. Wash your hands frequently to help prevent infections. Do not drive or operate heavy machinery if you feel dizzy or faint after your injection.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor immediately or go to the emergency room if you experience: sudden or severe pain in your left upper stomach or left shoulder (this could be a sign of a spleen problem); difficulty breathing, chest pain, or rapid heartbeat; severe bone or joint pain that does not improve with over-the-counter pain relievers; signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing; signs of infection such as fever over 100.4°F (38°C), chills, or body aches; painful, red, or swollen skin (which may be a sign of a rare skin condition called Sweet's syndrome); or any unusual or severe side effects.
when_it_works: This medicine starts working within 1 to 2 days of your injection by stimulating your bone marrow to produce more white blood cells. Your white blood cell count typically peaks within 3 to 4 days and then gradually returns to normal. You may not feel any different while the medicine is working, but your doctor will monitor your blood counts with lab tests.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. The risks and benefits should be discussed with your doctor before using this medicine. Children: This medicine can be used in children for certain conditions, but the dose may be different based on body weight. Your child's doctor will determine the right dose. Older adults: Older adults can generally use this medicine safely, but should report any unusual side effects to their doctor. Kidney or liver problems: No dose adjustment is usually needed, but inform your doctor about any kidney or liver conditions you have.
